summary.text: Take \(n=1408\) and exhaust all \(1\le k<1408\), writing \(N_k=(k+1)^{\phi(1408-k)/2}-k\): 1387 values have an explicit proper divisor, five endpoint values are directly nonprime, and the remaining 15 violate the prime-modulus Fermat congruence \(2^{N_k-1}\equiv1\pmod{N_k}\). Thus every candidate \(N_k\) is nonprime, so no required \(k\) exists for this \(n\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the second assertion in the conjecture.  The counterexample is
\[
                         n=1408.
\]
Thus it is enough to prove that, for every integer \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq1407\),
\[
 N_k=(k+1)^{e_k}-k,\qquad
 e_k=\left\lfloor\frac{\varphi(1408-k)}2\right\rfloor,
\]
is not prime.  (For the two values for which the exponent involves \(\varphi(1)\) or \(\varphi(2)\), the quotient by 2 is integer division, as in the statement being refuted.)

Here is the finite arithmetic computation establishing this.  It is described in detail so that the exhaustive portion of the argument is reproducible and so that its logical role is clear.

For each \(k=1,2,\ldots,1407\), first put \(m=1408-k\).  Factor \(m\) by trial division.  If
\[
                  m=\prod_i p_i^{a_i},
\]
then calculate
\[
                  \varphi(m)=\prod_i p_i^{a_i-1}(p_i-1)
\]
and set \(e_k=\lfloor\varphi(m)/2\rfloor\).  This gives the exponent without ever having to expand the usually enormous integer \((k+1)^{e_k}\).  Divisibility is then tested by modular binary exponentiation: to compute \(b^e\pmod q\), start with \(x=1\), \(y=b\bmod q\), read the binary digits of \(e\) from right to left, replace \(x\) by \(xy\bmod q\) whenever the current digit is 1, and replace \(y\) by \(y^2\bmod q\) after every digit.  After the first \(j\) digits have been read, the invariant is
\[
 x\,y^{\lfloor e/2^j\rfloor}\equiv b^e\pmod q.
\]
Consequently, when all digits have been read, the returned value really is \(b^e\bmod q\).  Thus a returned value \(k\bmod q\), on input \(b=k+1,e=e_k\), proves
\[
                         q\mid N_k.
\]
All comparisons needed below are ordinary integer comparisons.  In particular, every divisor used was also checked to satisfy \(1<q<N_k\).  The latter can be checked without decimal expansion: repeated squaring gives the exact binary expansion of \((k+1)^{e_k}\), after which subtraction of \(k\) and comparison with \(q\) are finite integer operations.

This calculation divides the 1407 possible values of \(k\) into three disjoint classes.

1. For 1387 values of \(k\), namely every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,1407\}\) except
\[
\begin{split}
E={}&\{84,125,221,354,438,459,621,623,665,852,914,986,1013,1026,1133\},\\
T={}&\{1402,1404,1405,1406,1407\},
\end{split}
\]
the modular-divisor calculation returns an integer \(d_k\) satisfying
\[
  1<d_k<N_k,
  \qquad (k+1)^{e_k}\equiv k\pmod {d_k}.
\]
Hence \(d_k\mid N_k\), so \(N_k\) is composite.

For clarity, this was a case-by-case divisor computation, not a probabilistic primality test.  There are 322 distinct returned divisors.  The most frequent ones provide useful independent checks on the sieve: \(d_k=3\) in 458 cases, \(7\) in 179 cases, \(5\) in 115 cases, \(11\) in 49 cases, \(13\) in 37 cases, \(19\) in 31 cases, \(23\) in 25 cases, \(17\) in 22 cases, \(67\) in 20 cases, \(31\) in 16 cases, \(37\) in 13 cases, \(47\) in 10 cases, \(29\) in 9 cases, and \(41\) in 8 cases.  The remaining returned divisors account for the other cases.  The counts add to 1387.  Some initial entries of the calculation, showing explicitly how the certificate is read, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k&e_k&d_k\\ \hline
1&396&3\\
2&324&31\\
3&560&13\\
4&216&3\\
5&660&8819\\
6&350&43\\
7&466&3\\
8&240&7\\
9&699&5867\\
10&232&3\\
11&630&529181351\\
12&348&47\\
13&360&3\\
14&320&47\\
15&594&7\\
16&224&3\\
17&636&171593370671\\
18&276&191\\
19&462&3\\
20&346&13679.
\end{array}
\]
For example, \(1408-1=1407=3\cdot7\cdot67\), so
\(
\varphi(1407)=2\cdot6\cdot66=792
\)
and \(e_1=396\).  Binary modular exponentiation gives \(2^{396}\equiv1\pmod3\), hence \(3\mid2^{396}-1\); the number is plainly larger than 3.  For \(k=2\),
\(1406=2\cdot19\cdot37\), so \(e_2=(1\cdot18\cdot36)/2=324\), and modular exponentiation gives \(3^{324}\equiv2\pmod {31}\), proving that 31 is a proper divisor of \(3^{324}-2\).  Every one of the other 1385 entries is checked in exactly the same fashion.  Near the other end of the range, the returned certificates include
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
1398&2&19\\
1399&3&19\\
1400&2&13\\
1401&3&7\\
1403&2&373.
\end{array}
\]
These also illustrate that no interval of possible \(k\)'s is omitted.

2. For the fifteen values in \(E\), no proper divisor was needed.  They are eliminated by a Fermat congruence.  The corresponding exponents are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr}
k&84&125&221&354&438&459&621&623&665&852&914&986&1013&1026&1133\\ \hline
e_k&330&641&593&240&192&432&393&312&371&138&108&105&156&95&100.
\end{array}
\]
For each column form \(N_k=(k+1)^{e_k}-k\).  Repeated squaring modulo \(N_k\), using the same binary algorithm described above, gives
\[
                         2^{N_k-1}\not\equiv1\pmod {N_k}.
\]
In each of these fifteen cases the calculation also gives \(N_k>2\).  To spell out why this proves compositeness, suppose that one of these \(N_k\) were prime.  Since \(N_k>2\), the residue class of 2 is nonzero modulo \(N_k\).  The nonzero residue classes modulo a prime form a multiplicative group of order \(N_k-1\).  Lagrange's theorem would therefore imply
\[
                         2^{N_k-1}\equiv1\pmod {N_k},
\]
contrary to the displayed modular computation.  Thus all fifteen of these \(N_k\)'s are nonprime.

For completeness, the modular calculation in this class does not assume the conclusion that \(N_k\) is composite.  The modulus \(N_k\) is first produced by exact exponentiation; its binary digits determine the exponent \(N_k-1\); and the square-and-multiply recurrence uses only multiplication and Euclidean remainders.  Its invariant proves at every stage that the stored residue is the appropriate power of 2.  The final residue was in each case strictly between 1 and \(N_k-1\), so it is not the residue 1.  Fermat's theorem is used only after this independent congruence computation.

As a sample check on the exponent table, for \(k=84\) one has
\[
1408-84=1324=2^2\cdot331,
\quad
\varphi(1324)=2(331-1)=660,
\quad e_{84}=330.
\]
For \(k=125\),
\[
1408-125=1283
\]
is prime, so \(\varphi(1283)=1282\) and \(e_{125}=641\).  The other thirteen exponents follow from the same displayed product formula for the totient.

3. It remains to deal with \(T\), where the values are small enough to evaluate directly.  They are:

* If \(k=1402\), then \(1408-k=6\), \(\varphi(6)=2\), and therefore \(e_k=1\).  Hence
\[
N_{1402}=1403-1402=1.
\]

* If \(k=1404\), then \(1408-k=4\), \(\varphi(4)=2\), and \(e_k=1\).  Hence
\[
N_{1404}=1405-1404=1.
\]

* If \(k=1405\), then \(1408-k=3\), \(\varphi(3)=2\), and \(e_k=1\).  Hence
\[
N_{1405}=1406-1405=1.
\]

* If \(k=1406\), then \(1408-k=2\), \(\varphi(2)=1\), so \(e_k=\lfloor1/2\rfloor=0\).  Thus the formal natural-number subtraction in the conjecture gives \(1-1406=0\); with ordinary integer subtraction it gives a negative integer.  Either way it is not a positive prime.

* If \(k=1407\), then \(1408-k=1\), \(\varphi(1)=1\), again \(e_k=0\), and \(1-1407\) is likewise 0 under truncated natural subtraction and negative under integer subtraction.  It is not prime.

The three classes are disjoint and contain respectively 1387, 15, and 5 integers, totaling
\[
                         1387+15+5=1407.
\]
They therefore exhaust every integer \(k\) satisfying \(0<k<1408\).  In every case \(N_k\) is nonprime.  Consequently there is no positive \(k<1408\) for which
\[
                  (k+1)^{\varphi(1408-k)/2}-k
\]
is prime.

Finally, \(1408>5\).  The conjecture asserts that such a \(k\) exists for every \(n>5\), so its assertion at \(n=1408\) is false.  Since the full OEIS conjecture is the conjunction of that universal assertion with the separate assertion \(a(n)>0\) for all \(n>1\), falsity of this second conjunct already disproves the conjunction; nothing about the first conjunct is needed.
